{{Nihongo|'''Jun John Sakurai'''|桜井 純|Sakurai Jun|January 31, 1933 – November 1, 1982}} was a Japanese–American theoretical particle physicist.

While a graduate student at Cornell University, Sakurai independently discovered the V-A theory of weak interactions.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Nambu, Yoichiro|authorlink=Yoichiro Nambu|title=Obituary: Jun John Sakurai|journal=Physics Today|date=February 1983|volume=36|issue=2|pages=87|doi=10.1063/1.2915507|bibcode=1983PhT....36b..87N|doi-access=free}}</ref>

He authored the popular graduate text ''[[Modern Quantum Mechanics]]'' (1985, published posthumously) and other texts such as ''Invariance Principles and Elementary Particles'' (1964) and ''Advanced Quantum Mechanics'' (1967).

==Life and career==

J. J. Sakurai was born in [[Tokyo]] in 1933 and moved to the United States when he was a high school student. He studied physics at Harvard and Cornell, where he proposed his theory of weak interactions. After receiving his PhD from Cornell in 1958 he joined the faculty at University of Chicago, becoming a full professor in 1964.<ref name="auto">J. J. Sakurai, San Fu Tuan. ''Modern Quantum Mechanics'': Revised Edition. Pearson Education, 1994. pg. vii</ref>  In 1970, Sakurai moved to the University of California, Los Angeles.

As a graduate student, he proposed the [[V−A theory]] of weak interactions, independently of [[Robert Marshak]], [[George Sudarshan]], [[Richard Feynman]], and [[Murray Gell-Mann]]. In 1960,  he published a paper<ref>Sakurai, J. J. (1960). "Theory of strong interactions", ''Annals of Physics'' '''11''' (1), 1-48.</ref> on the theory of strong interactions based on Abelian and non-Abelian ([[Yang–Mills theory|Yang-Mills]]) gauge invariance.

In that paper, he also  pioneered the [[vector meson dominance]] model of hadron dynamics.<ref name="auto"/>

Sakurai died from an [[aneurysm]] in 1982 during a visit to CERN.<ref name=sternheimer>{{cite conference|title=Fond memories of Julian and Clarice, especially involving Moshe Flato and Noriko Sakurai |last1=Sternheimer |first1=Daniel |author-link1= |date=2019 |publisher= |book-title=Proceedings Of The Julian Schwinger Centennial Conference |pages=279 |location= |conference= Julian Schwinger Centennial Conference|id=}}</ref>

==Textbooks==

In addition to his published papers, Sakurai authored several textbooks. These include ''Invariance Principles and Elementary Particles'' (1964), ''Advanced Quantum Mechanics'' (1967), and ''Modern Quantum Mechanics''. The third volume was left unfinished due to Sakurai's sudden death in 1982, but was later edited and completed with the help of his wife, Noriko Sakurai, and colleague San Fu Tuan.<ref>J. J. Sakurai, San Fu Tuan. ''Modern Quantum Mechanics'': Revised Edition. Pearson Education, 1994. pg. iii</ref> ''Modern Quantum Mechanics'' is probably his most well known book and is still widely used for graduate studies today.<ref>{{Cite book |isbn = 978-0805382914|title = Modern Quantum Mechanics|last1 = Sakurai|first1 = Jun John|last2 = Napolitano|first2 = Jim|year = 2011| publisher=Addison-Wesley }}</ref>

==Sakurai Prize==

In 1984 the family and friends of J. J. Sakurai endowed a prize for theoretical physicists in his honor. The goal of the prize as stated on the [[American Physical Society|APS]] website is to encourage outstanding work in the field of particle theory. Recipients receive a $10,000 grant, an allowance for travel to the ceremony, and a certificate citing their contributions to particle physics.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/sakurai.cfm |title = J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics}}</ref>
